description: We are Marco Zero, a team of Artificial Intelligence students from CIn/UFPE in Recife, Brazil. At the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, we chose Be An Earth System Trend Detective!, which explores environmental changes through scientific data. We aim to build a tool to identify, analyze, and visualize environmental trends with statistical rigor. Our interests include AI, programming, data science, and web development, as well as Earth science and science communication.
summary:
One extreme rainfall event raises a bigger question: is our climate changing, or are we seeing a short-term fluctuation?

TRACE — Follow the Evidence is an interactive climate investigation platform developed by Team Marco Zero for the challenge "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!"

Using NASA POWER and Giovanni/MERRA-2 data for Recife, Brazil (1991–2024), TRACE helps users compare historical climate periods, examine temperature and precipitation trends, and explore the conditions preceding documented rainfall events.

Our approach combines reproducible statistical analysis, uncertainty estimates, historical evidence, and scientific limitations. Rather than treating a single chart as proof, TRACE encourages users to question results, inspect data sources, and distinguish observations from unsupported conclusions.

TRACE transforms complex Earth science data into an accessible investigation, helping people understand not only what climate evidence reveals, but also what it cannot establish.
details:
TRACE — Follow the Evidence

Team: Marco Zero

Challenge: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!

THE PROBLEM

Extreme weather events often lead to a difficult question: are we observing long-term environmental change, natural variability, or an isolated event?

A single rainfall episode cannot establish a climate trend. Even a statistically significant result requires careful interpretation, transparent methods, and an understanding of uncertainty.

TRACE was created to make this scientific investigation more accessible.

OUR SOLUTION

TRACE — Follow the Evidence is an interactive web application that transforms NASA Earth science data into an evidence-based investigation.

Our initial case study focuses on Recife, Pernambuco, Brazil, using historical climate observations from 1991 to 2024.

The platform allows users to investigate two environmental indicators: near-surface air temperature and precipitation.

The goal is not simply to display climate graphs, but to help users understand the evidence behind environmental trends.

HOW TRACE WORKS

The platform follows an interactive scientific investigation:

Discover → Investigate → Challenge → Reveal → Verdict

  1. Discover

Users begin with an environmental question and select the climate indicator they want to examine.

  1. Investigate

TRACE uses historical NASA climate datasets to compare different time periods and examine how environmental indicators change over time.

The statistical engine applies Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression with Heteroskedasticity and Autocorrelation Consistent (HAC/Newey–West) inference.

Results include trend estimates, 95% confidence intervals, p-values, and sensitivity checks using different HAC lag settings.

  1. Challenge

Rather than accepting a trend automatically, users are encouraged to examine uncertainty, compare analytical windows, and consider limitations.

This step helps distinguish statistically supported findings from inconclusive evidence.

  1. Reveal

TRACE presents the underlying observations, visualizations, statistical results, data provenance, and methodological explanations.

The application also includes an investigation of climate conditions before documented historical events.

For example, users can examine the ten days preceding the May 28, 2022 rainfall event in Recife. The NASA-derived dataset records 156.20 mm of accumulated precipitation during May 18–27, 2022.

These observations describe the selected period; they do not establish that the preceding conditions caused the event.

  1. Verdict

The application communicates evidence-based conclusions through deterministic classification rules grounded in the established statistical methodology.

The verdicts communicate the strength and limitations of the available evidence rather than claiming absolute certainty.

HISTORICAL EVENT INVESTIGATION

In addition to long-term climate trends, TRACE includes an interactive investigation of the ten calendar days preceding selected historical events.

Users can explore daily observations, climate charts, documented event references, and downloadable CSV/JSON data.

The team also developed a separate reproducible retrospective study of five historical episodes in Recife, using seasonally aligned reference windows.

This comparative research is documented as a scientific artifact rather than presented as a live predictive system.

NASA DATA AND SCIENTIFIC METHODOLOGY

TRACE uses two NASA data services.

NASA POWER provides corrected MERRA-2 precipitation data (PRECTOTCORR).

NASA Giovanni / MERRA-2 provides daily mean near-surface air temperature data (T2MMEAN).

The datasets cover 1991–2024 and are processed through documented, reproducible workflows.

The project preserves source files, processing scripts, scientific documentation, and automated tests.

Our analysis explicitly addresses uncertainty, data completeness, spatial coverage, and the limitations of statistical inference.

TECHNOLOGY

TRACE was developed using Python, FastAPI, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, and statsmodels for backend services and scientific analysis.

The interactive frontend was developed using React, TypeScript, and Vite.

GitHub was used for version control, documentation, and automated validation.

The frontend is hosted on GitHub Pages, while the API is deployed on Render.

The application is designed to make scientific results understandable to people without specialized statistical training while preserving the underlying methodology.

CREATIVITY AND IMPACT

TRACE's main contribution is the combination of scientific analysis with an interactive investigation in which the user is encouraged to question the evidence.

Instead of presenting a climate trend as an unquestionable conclusion, TRACE connects observations, statistical uncertainty, historical context, and reproducible methodology.

This approach can support environmental education, scientific literacy, and more responsible interpretation of Earth observation data.

SCIENTIFIC LIMITATIONS

TRACE is an exploratory scientific tool.

It does not predict disasters, establish causal relationships, issue early warnings, or provide operational risk probabilities.

The NASA datasets are gridded climate products, not direct measurements from weather stations at the sites of historical impacts. Their exact common spatial coverage has not been established.

Historical comparisons are descriptive and retrospective; they should not be interpreted as validated predictive models.

These limitations are intentionally communicated to promote transparency and responsible scientific interpretation.

PROJECT ACCESS

Live application:
https://victor-tenorio.github.io/trace-follow-the-evidence/

Source code and reproducibility documentation:
https://github.com/victor-tenorio/trace-follow-the-evidence
